en: Khan, what fiery lowland is this?
Having seen flesh, he would sever the head,
What would he not do to stone!
He had often seen heads severed,
What is so very near?
You are no less than a dragon,
Like a cutting blow from Azar Kaysan,
At the word 'horse,' his riding seemed ready to launch,
As though Boshono could defend a thousand,
The one he encountered seemed fierce,
Whoever met him seemed doomed,
Enslaving whoever encountered him,
As though setting the burned one upon the ground,
A tower like a hero,
The Arab of the tower,
At the foot of the tower,
A lone white yurt stands below,
Two khans whose paths met,
Did no traveler come?
Someone is riding along at a steady pace,
This hero is Karakhan,
No one who saw it could remain standing,
Now it seems beyond all reach,
The tiger stands in fury,
The hapless one stands, unable to remain,
His fangs stand ready for torment,
The calamity this one has brought,
Have you seen it from this daughter of yours?
How many lands he drew troops against,
Striking him, the wicked black host,
Many are his raiding marches,
His great ones rode at the head,
The misery of those who cherish life,
He has a bone made for toil,
He burned it down to the roots,
Of the man who looked swiftly,
His heart was torn within him,
His teeth themselves are strong,
What is called his arm grew strong,
He satisfied the sorcerer,
Comparing him to Chubak's son,
Gathering without finding a champion,
Not building it for one unworthy,
Appearing mighty in courage,
A weak soul without courage,
He died before his destined hour,
Stirring bloodshed and gathering the people,
With his waters, truth descended,
The punishment of the Chinese people,
Have the third one delivered into their hands,
A khan's command is never twofold,
Is there anyone who will fight?
His courage is equal to three hundred,
Then his son stood there unharmed,
[Uncertain: Turning his eyes to the right,]
With sickle-curved brows,
[Uncertain: Sitting there himself in agitation,]
If you would see a marvel, look at this!
Gathering every last seer,
[Uncertain: He gathered those versed in hidden things,]
[Uncertain: If he would not give his judgment,]
If he would not obey what was said,
[Uncertain: He had made their blood run dark,]
[Uncertain: Hardship came upon their lives,]
Suurulgan, who had devised a plan,
When Suurulgan gave the order,
The teeming Kytai, the people of forty khans,
Were sorely distressed.
“Where will he drive us?” they wondered,
Fearing he would do such a deed again,
Bringing misery upon many people,
[Uncertain: Fearing he would slaughter them in punishment,]
His great wrath became apparent,
Even his valiant warriors,
Despairing of their precious lives,
All surged about in an uproar,
The army poured forth,
Their clamor rose to the sky.
All that was old was indeed old,
All that struck the stone was pierced,
Ear pressed against ear,
They moved in a swarm, clamoring like worms,
They asked what land and what kind it was,
Some souls went off in bewilderment,
Before long, some were astonished,
As he traveled among the people,
As he stood for the people,
In the royal city of Kökükö,
The people thronged and shone like ore,
On the blue hill stood a tower,
Do not ask about the tower,
If you ask about the tower,
In the khan’s land of China,
When the khan appeared before them,
When he was to issue an order,
The people clamored, the nation roared,
When they were to see the khan’s face,
The tower served as a signal,
Do not ask about its tower,
Nine thousand ears all listened,
Upon it was a signal bell,
When its bell was struck,
Across a distance of nine days,’ travel,
It was heard like a mighty wind,
The bell was its signal,
It rang until ears were deafened,
All the people under the sun,
Marveled at this tumult,
They stood watching, crowded together,
While the people stood astonished,
He emerged as though drawn forth,
At his menace, souls took fright,
At his visage, the blood drained away,
What a figure he proved to be,
His equal was truly his match,
Most valiant, with fierce wrath,
With a head like a small cauldron,
With brows like a recumbent camel,
With teeth like a whip,
His face loomed as vast as the whole world,
His crown stood sharp against the rain,
He had a head broad as the back of a palm,
In battle his face thrust forward,
He did not fear one who answered back,
When he merely flicked his brow,
He laid low every foe he seized,
He made his own name mighty,
When he merely knit his brow,
He disgraced them on the spot.
At his menace, men died of fright,
His visage blazed with wrath,
No man could endure approaching him,
A man spoken of like a wild beast,
Such a man stood there.
His executioners numbered seven hundred,
He had four thousand nobles,
His guards had their appointed fortune,
They stood with swords drawn.
Guards for the treasury,
Finishing their words, they fell silent,
The short of the angry words was this,
The chiefs who would not disperse,
When the decree remained, he cried out,
He had risen since the dawn,
They would not tell him to turn back to his horse,
They would not go and cause distress,
Now among the Chinese of forty kinds,
His disordered muttering,
They would not remain to turn back with a shout.
Ever a khan to the enemy people,
Murmuring in submission,
Pouring out and raking over your airs,
Cast down beneath,
His splendor looked like a mountain,
With arms as massive as a cart,
His excellence was his courage,
He appeared as one son of humankind.
Here too were two khans,
Now the chosen ones of the forty clans,
The son of the forty maidens,
The gathered Chinese stood watching,
We were the ones who stood out,
Here stood Ysyk-Tekur,
Was he the blue-maned gray,
One grave word from Koloy,
As though endowed with great courage,
Did the great one go striking with his sword,
As though he went with the valiant one.
When the third stood here,
To continue the tale briefly,
Of the Chinese, of distant Kakan,
He gathered its teeming people,
When Suurman stood there,
There was no one to turn them back,
His treasury remained unbroken,
When he took the reckoning,
There was no city besides Kakan,
When the teeming Chinese remained,
Third, to Dyisha,
His son, the city’s herald,
The khan’s night had fallen,
There was no one at all to guard the frontier,
Look closely: this people is Beijing,
Koloy’s grim, dark might,
This black host belongs to Dyisha,
He has a people swarming like black worms,
All the people of forty tribes are there,
The elder of all the people,
The ablest of the spearmen,
The finest of those who mount the troop,
This is the pasha of Beijing,
The tent of the watchman,
The hero of the people of Kakan,
Together with Suurulma and Chyng Tengir,
There are two heroes who win the horses,
Their names resound among the people,
They are a blessing to us,
There is a pair of heroes,
While the two of us stand here,
Would some grim mighty foe confront us?
Would one who has gone as an equal strike us?
Could an enemy break the heroes?
Would a man turn back without dying?
The people called him their enemy,
No living soul had defeated his might,
The lineage of two daughters,
A descendant of brave Kökchö,
His thought of the enemy was keen,
Of these scattered Burut people,
Look at the descendant who remained,
They say they set out upon that journey,
This fleeting world of seven days,
They say its course is sorrow,
The person who goes does not return,
He has entered the dark grave,
Word passes down from sage to sage,
The finest of them, a young champion,
From the great branch that would remain with Kerimche,
I heard that no offspring remained,
Among peoples of many different ranks,
One named Kenen was born,
I heard that a descendant remained.
Making Ala-Too his homeland,
I heard that Kongur remained,
When he went to Karakuman,
When Kaltai attacked from his side,
Fleeing, he saved the khan alive,
Laying a claim against Kaltai,
I heard that he took his blood in vengeance.
Advancing three times from the right flank,
They say he waged a boundless battle,
Firing the great jazayil and the bow,
They say the wretched Kyrgyz attacked.
The Örötkül came and moved around them,
The Chinese who went unpunished,
Ambushing them in a hidden place and striking them down,
Scattering all their possessions,
The Örötkül then turned back.
Turning back the edge of that host,
Their hero was Badykan,
That glaring Chinese warrior,
With no soul left to answer back,
That ill-fated eagle,
Casting them down as though slaughtered,
Without looking any man in the face,
Black-headed and fork-footed,
Unable to reckon a man worth even coarse cloth,
Having every passerby bound,
Bringing down the leopard-like khan.
From the man who went to meet them,
He has wrung the news from him.
His heroism and princely bearing,
He is a warrior better than them all,
A man who traveled there has seen him,
To every eye that beholds him, he is wondrous,
He roamed among peoples and reconnoitered lands,
